short: The engineer who wrapped the tracks around the hull and later made tanks drivable.
full:
Walter Gordon Wilson was born at Blackrock near Dublin, took a first in mechanical sciences at Cambridge, and built experimental aero engines with the aviation pioneer Percy Pilcher before turning to motor cars: the Wilson-Pilcher of 1900 had a flat engine and an epicyclic gearbox running in oil. In 1914 he was with the Royal Naval Air Service armoured car squadrons, which is how he came to the Landships Committee and to Foster's of Lincoln.

Wilson's contribution to the first tank was the shape itself. Instead of a tracked chassis with a body on top, he carried the track all the way around a tall rhomboid hull, so the leading face met a parapet at the height of the climb; the guns went into side sponsons to keep the top clear. That machine was Mother. He returned to gearboxes afterwards, and his epicyclic steering gear let one man drive the Mark V where four had been needed. His self-changing gearbox, patented in 1928, went into buses, cars and later British tanks.
